result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.k_truss()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Extract the k-truss subgraph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L28249-L28330){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.k_truss(k) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![k-truss](/assets/graphs/k-truss.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: the eight-node graph with a dense cluster A to D, a ring E, F, G and a pendant H. Right: the 3-truss keeps only edges that lie in a triangle: the six edges of A to D plus C to E and D to E, in the accent color. The chordless loop through F and G and the pendant edge are in no triangle and are dashed, along with F, G, H." width="100%"} The k-truss is the maximal subgraph where every edge is part of at least `(k-2)` triangles. Iteratively removes edges with insufficient triangle support. Removing an edge can destroy triangles that other edges relied on, so pruning repeats until every remaining edge has enough support. Nodes left without any edges are then dropped. Because it is based on triangles rather than degrees, the k-truss is a stricter notion of cohesion than the k-core: every k-truss is contained in the `(k-1)`-core, but a k-core can contain sparse, triangle-free structures that a truss rejects. The k-truss is useful for: - extracting tightly knit groups in social or collaboration networks, where friends of friends tend to be friends - finding dense functional modules in biological networks - cleaning up a graph before community detection by removing edges that are not embedded in any triangle (`k=3`) Each round recounts the triangles on every remaining edge, so the method can be slow on large, dense graphs. Edge weights are ignored. The method is intended for undirected graphs; on a directed graph, triangles are counted from the out-neighbors of each edge's endpoints. The original graph is not modified. The returned graph keeps node labels and edge weights, but node IDs are reassigned (use labels to match nodes back to the original) and other node and edge attributes are not copied. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [k]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Minimum number of triangles + 2 for edges. Must be >= 3. `k=3` keeps every edge that lies in at least one triangle, `k=4` requires two triangles per edge, and so on. A complete graph on `n` nodes is an `n`-truss. If no edge qualifies, the result is an empty graph. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : New graph containing only the k-truss edges and their endpoints. Isolated nodes are removed. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If k < 3. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} The graph below has a dense cluster (A, B, C, D, every pair connected), a loop through E, F, and G, and a pendant node H. The 3-truss keeps only the edges that are part of a triangle: the cluster plus the triangle C-D-E. The edges through F, G, and H belong to no triangle, so those nodes disappear: ::: {#5b03c999 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G", "H"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("A", "D"), ("B", "C"), ("B", "D"), ("C", "D"), ("C", "E"), ("D", "E"), ("E", "F"), ("F", "G"), ("G", "D"), ("G", "H")]) ) truss_3 = graph.k_truss(3) (sorted(truss_3.get_node_df()["label"].to_list()), truss_3.count_edges()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E'], 8) ``` ::: ::: In the 4-truss every edge must lie in at least two triangles. The edges C-E and D-E are in only one, so E drops out and just the cluster's six edges remain: ::: {#3ecb2458 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} truss_4 = graph.k_truss(4) (sorted(truss_4.get_node_df()["label"].to_list()), truss_4.count_edges()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (['A', 'B', 'C', 'D'], 6) ``` ::: :::
